answers.text: The instruction I'd give: three lines every time, in order — delivery date, item and quantity, and any change, saying 'no change' if there isn't one. If something's missing, say the date not confirmed, I'd put 'not confirmed' rather than guessing. It comes out the same each time because the three lines are always there.
Tell it: one line per claim — date, amount, category, person — same order every time, then a total at the bottom that's the sum of the amount column for the week.

The price bit is fine, 100 times €48.50 really is €4,850. The issue is the dates — call on the 14th, delivery revised to the 19th, but it also says the 19th is 'three days out from today', which would only work if today was the 16th, and that doesn't sit right next to a call on the 14th. I'd want that checked before it's sent.
62 up from 54 checks out, about 15%. But 3 late out of 62 works out closer to 95%, not the 97% written here.

I'd sign off the second one — it shows €612,000 and €25,100 and the working, so you can see where 4.1% comes from. The first is just a number on its own; if it's wrong there's nothing in the sentence to show it. Might well be right, it's just not possible to tell either way as it stands.

I'd send the second one, the order and credit references are right there so anyone can check exactly what was done later. The first says 'this was entirely our error' without anything behind it, so that line can't be checked as written. Not necessarily wrong, it would just want a look-over first.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. Yes, already public. 5. No.

The pricing and discount terms I wouldn't paste straight in, that's the sensitive part. The confidentiality clause too, since it names both companies directly. The delivery schedule is fine as is, nothing sensitive about dates on their own. I'd leave the registration details out as well, just to be safe.

Before it goes to the manager I'd check the delivery total and the on-time figure straight against the warehouse system, not just read the sentence over. I'd do it every week, right after the draft's written and before it's sent up, checking a couple of numbers against source each time. That would pick up a wrong total, not just a spelling slip.

Step 4 is where the gate needs to be — once the confirmation goes out automatically there's no pulling it back if something upstream was wrong. Step 1 carries risk too, a wrong item there runs through everything after it, but step 4 is where it actually reaches the customer. The gate should hold anything where the stock check is right at the edge, or the quantity looks unusually high for a normal order.
